opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a pretty reasonable objection, and I feel some of the pull of it myself.

The basic picture we've had in mind is something like: you have a model, and alongside it you want to learn an explanation for why the model behaves the way it does. Ideally you'd find that explanation the same way you found the model, by gradient descent over some big parameterized space. That's the only approach we know that really scales. If we needed humans, or some discrete combinatorial search, to construct explanations, we'd never keep pace with how fast models are being trained.

But explanations don't obviously look like things that live in a nice continuous space. When I think of an explanation, I picture something discrete and structured. "This circuit computes this feature, and these two features are roughly independent, so their product behaves like this." That's built out of claims and inferences. Whether you include a particular argument isn't a dial you turn smoothly from zero to one. So you might worry that once you embed explanations in a continuous space, the space is mostly filled with garbage that doesn't correspond to anything, and the meaningful points are a measure-zero set you'll never find by gradient descent.

There's a second worry, which I think is the more serious one. If you search over a rich continuous space of "explanations" and optimize some objective, like how well the explanation predicts the model's behavior, you may simply find whatever exploits the objective. You get something that scores well but isn't really an explanation in the sense we care about. It's not tracking the reasons the model does what it does. It's another black box that happens to fit. Then you've lost the whole point, which was to have something that tells you when the model's behavior on a new input happens for a different reason than on the training distribution.

So my position is roughly this. I think those objections are real, and they're part of why we've spent so much time on the more theoretical side: what is a heuristic explanation, formally, and what properties should it have? If you understand the object well, you can hope to design a parameterization where the continuous relaxation is natural, where nearby points are nearby explanations, rather than hoping it just works out. There's some precedent. Neural nets themselves are a weird continuous relaxation of programs, and that turned out far better than most people would have guessed. But I wouldn't stake much on the analogy. Our confidence that it works here is pretty low until we actually have the definitions nailed down, and that's still the hard part.

r001.rationale: The response says explanations contain discrete claims and that including an argument is not a smooth dial, but it does not clearly state that small changes to a valid simple explanation can make it fail.

r002.rationale: The response discusses gradient descent over explanation spaces and neural nets as a program analogy, but does not address feature directions in simple models or whether that approach extends to a human brain doing logical reasoning.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the objection goes something like this. When we talk about explanations, or proofs, or arguments, we're usually talking about discrete objects. A proof is a sequence of steps. An explanation is a story about why something happens. And there's a kind of rigidity to that, where either the steps are valid or they aren't, and you can check them. The worry is that once you say, okay, instead of searching over discrete explanations, we're going to search over some continuous space of things that we're going to call explanations, you lose a lot of what made the concept useful in the first place.

And I think the sharpest version of the concern is that continuous optimization is really good at finding things that satisfy whatever criterion you wrote down, without necessarily having the property you actually cared about. So if I say an explanation is something that lets me predict the model's behavior, or something that accounts for some fraction of the variance, and then I do gradient descent over a parameterized family to find the thing that scores best, the default outcome is that I get something that scores well on my metric and is not really an explanation in any deep sense. It's just another model. I've trained a second neural network that approximates the first one, and I'm no closer to understanding anything. That's a very reasonable thing to be worried about, and I think it's basically the central technical risk of the whole approach.

There's a second version of the concern that's more philosophical, which is that the thing we wanted from explanations was something like compositionality. You want to be able to take an explanation of this piece and an explanation of that piece and combine them. Discrete symbolic objects do that naturally. Continuous things sort of don't. If I have a vector that explains one behavior and another vector that explains another, it's not obvious what it means to glue them together or check them against each other.

So I take both of those seriously. Where I end up is not that the objection is wrong, but that I don't think the discrete alternative is actually available. If you look at what neural networks actually do, the structure that's there is continuous. The features are continuous, the relationships between them are approximately linear in some directions and messy in others, and when people try to extract clean discrete circuits, what they tend to find is that the clean story accounts for some of the behavior and then there's a long tail of stuff that doesn't fit. You can either throw up your hands at that point, or you can say, okay, the explanation itself needs to be able to represent approximate and partial structure, which basically means it has to live in a continuous space.

So my view is more like, the objection correctly identifies a cost, and the question is whether you can pay the cost and still get what you wanted. And the way you'd try to do that is by being much more careful about what the explanation has to accomplish, so that the degenerate solutions, the ones where you've just trained a second model, actually fail the criterion. That's hard, and I don't think we've nailed it, but I think it's the right problem to be working on rather than hoping the discrete version pans out.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something to the objection that, when we understand something, we’re often finding a discrete structure—a program or an argument—and it’s not obvious how to get there by gradually improving a candidate explanation. If your explanation has ten steps and one of them is wrong, the whole thing may fail. It’s not clear that making that step a little less wrong gives you a useful signal about where to go next.

So I sympathize with that as an objection to a particular picture of how learning works. You can’t just say, “We have this continuous space, and we’ll do gradient descent,” and assume that explains how you discover a new concept or a new algorithm.

But I’m much less convinced that it establishes a limitation of neural networks. A neural network can learn to carry out a search over discrete objects. The continuous optimization is then learning the machinery that does the search, rather than directly searching over explanations. And humans also seem to acquire useful partial intuitions before they have a complete explanation. So there is some kind of intermediate signal available. The question is how effectively a learning process can use it.

r001.rationale: It says a multi-step explanation can fail when one step is wrong and that making the step only a little less wrong may not provide a useful direction, presenting this as an objection to gradual search through a continuous space.

r002.rationale: The response discusses gradient descent and neural networks generally, but does not express doubt about extending feature-direction discovery in simple models to interpreting a human brain doing logical reasoning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic concern is that the space of explanations has a lot of discrete structure. You might explain something by saying, “This circuit is implementing this algorithm,” and there isn’t necessarily a meaningful explanation halfway between that algorithm and some other algorithm. So if your plan is to write down a space of explanations and do gradient descent over it, it’s reasonable to ask whether you’ve represented the things you actually care about, or just some continuous proxy that’s easier to optimize.

That said, I don’t think the discreteness by itself is a decisive objection. Neural networks can learn to do tasks with lots of discrete structure. You could have a continuously parameterized system that proposes explanations, even if the explanations it proposes are discrete. The harder question is what objective tells you that an explanation is good. Does it actually capture why the model behaves the way it does, or does it just sound plausible and predict some observations? I’m more sympathetic to the objection when it’s pointing at that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says there may be no meaningful explanation halfway between two algorithms, but it does not say that small changes to a valid simple explanation can make it fail as an objection to continuous parameterization.
